What drives the work I choose to do? I've been a physicist, then became a data scientist, and along the way I've developed a fairly clear sense of what I want to spend my time on. Three ideas keep coming back, and they all happen to start with E.

![](image.jpg)

### Equity

Not equity in the financial sense — equity as in fairness and justice. I grew up in the Netherlands with a lot of advantages I didn't earn: citizenship, education, stable family. That background took a while to fully appreciate. The more I learned about how colonialism, racism, and structural inequality shape life outcomes, the harder it became to work on things that don't engage with that somehow.

Climate justice is a good example of where this gets concrete: the people most affected by environmental damage are rarely those most responsible for it.

### Ecology

Things are connected. That's the core of it. Ecology as a value means taking systems thinking seriously — not just in the biological sense, but in how economies, communities, and institutions interact. Diversity, circular systems, long feedback loops: these matter.

It also just means I'd rather work outdoors than not, and I find organisms more interesting than most software.

### Evidence

I like data. I think clearly gathered and honestly presented evidence is one of the better tools we have for making decisions and having arguments. Which is not to say data is neutral — it isn't — but the discipline of being honest about uncertainty and transparent about methods is worth something.

This is probably why I ended up as a data scientist.

### In practice

These three things together mean I look for work that uses careful analysis to address real inequity or ecological problems. That's the short version of why I do what I do.
